> 「如来昔在然灯佛所，于法有所得不？」「不也，世尊！如来在然灯佛所，于法实无所得。」……「应无所住而生其心。」

The tenth section is where the sutra states its central instruction in full, and it arrives by an unexpected route: a question about the past, a question about landscaping, and then one sentence that the rest of the text will keep returning to.

## 然灯佛 and the absence of receipt

The Buddha asks whether, in the far past, when 然灯佛 — Dīpaṃkara, the Buddha who prophesied his future awakening — he obtained any dharma.

须菩提 answers: no, nothing was obtained.

The interesting thing is that the tradition remembers this event as a formal prediction, a授记: a buddha declares that this person will become a buddha, with a name and an age. The sutra does not deny the event. It denies that anything was handed over.

A prediction is a description given at the right moment. It is not a transfer of property. If you received a certificate and mistook it for the thing certified, you would spend the rest of your life guarding the paper.

## 庄严佛土者，即非庄严，是名庄严

Then: does a bodhisattva adorn a buddha-land? No — because adorning a buddha-land is not adorning, therefore it is called adorning.

A buddha-land, in this literature, is the world that appears to a mind as it is purified. Adorning it means the work of making a world fit to be lived in: building, teaching, cleaning, arranging, caring for the people in it.

The section does not cancel that work. It cancels the version of it that has an external target: a place, finished, perfect, and visibly mine.

The book's phrasing is exact — the work continues, the photograph of the finished result does not get taken. Which is the only sustainable way to keep working: the moment your peace depends on the landscaping being complete, the landscaping has become a burden and the peace is conditional on something you cannot control.

## 应无所住而生其心

And then the sentence.

Two clauses again, and again they pull in opposite directions:

- 无所住 — not abiding: not sticking to form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or the objects of mind.
- 而生其心 — and yet giving rise to the mind.

The second clause is the one that gets dropped in translation, and dropping it turns the sutra into quietism. Something is to be generated: the mind of clarity, of compassion, of attention. Not the absence of mind.

The structure is therefore not "empty your mind and stay empty". It is: an active mind, with nothing underneath it holding it up. 生心 and 不住 are simultaneous — which is why the Chinese puts them in one breath rather than two sentences.

The book's warning about this sentence: any method that produces stillness by suppressing activity has misread 生. Any method that produces activity without noticing where it is stuck has misread 住.

## 须弥山王 and the great body

The section ends with a question about a body as large as Mount Sumeru, the mountain at the centre of the old cosmology. Great? Very great — because what the Buddha calls a body is not a body, therefore it is called a great body.

The great body is not a bigger flesh. It is the unimpeded, boundless body of the dharma — which has no boundary to be large across. Size requires edges. This has none.

The image is there to close the section the way it opened: nothing obtained, nothing decorated, nothing measured. A boundless body cannot be a possession.

## The test

Take something you are building. A body of work, a home, a practice, a reputation.

Ask: if it stopped halfway — right here, unfinished — would the mind that built it still stand?

If the answer is no, you have located where the mind is abiding. The building is fine. The abiding is the thing to see.
